item.title: What Drives Conspiracy Theories and the Psychology Behind It
item.description:
Conspiracy Theories

What Drives Conspiracy Theories and the Psychology Behind It

The psychology of conspiracy theorists.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • Belief in conspiracy theories is related to the believers’ extreme overconfidence.
  • Social psychological processes, such as specific biases, also strengthen conspiracy theorists’ beliefs.
  • The antidote is to provide as much objective, contradictory evidence as you can.

The Apollo moon landings never happened and were staged in Hollywood film studios.

Climate change and COVID-19 are hoaxes.

Feminism is a conspiracy to decrease the white birth rate to endanger the West.

These and many more conspiracy theories, both ones proven false and some true ones (e.g., for decades, tobacco companies buried evidence that smoking is deadly), were used in research to test people’s tendency to believe conspiracy theories.

Part of this research looked at the motivations, personality, and social identities of persons prone to believing conspiracy theories. In some of this research, belief in conspiracy theories is linked to narcissism and a desire to be seen as unique. There is also evidence that conspiracy believers tend to lack critical thinking skills. Some conspiracy theorists consider themselves to be “critical freethinkers” and reject the term “conspiracy theorist.”

Recent research (Pennycook et al., 2026) explored information processing factors that lead people to believe in, and adhere to, their belief in conspiracy theories. One of the strongest findings was that people who are prone to believe in conspiracy theories are extremely overconfident in their judgments and beliefs. Moreover, this overconfidence was most strongly related to the most extreme, “fringe” conspiracy theories. These same individuals tend to massively overestimate how much others agree with their beliefs. Even though conspiracy theory believers are in the minority (only 12 percent of the participants), they thought themselves to be in the majority 93 percent of the time. In short, not only do these individuals believe outlandish things, but they are sure that others do as well.

What Are Some of the Other Psychological Factors Involved?

Social psychology has clearly shown that we have certain ingrained biases in our thought processes that lead our normal, objective thinking astray. These biases serve not only to lead people to believe outlandish things, but they also strengthen those odd views.

Cognitive dissonance: This is the unpleasant state of inconsistencies in behaviors or in thoughts that humans tend to try to get rid of—we want to avoid these mental contradictions. So, we try to make sense of them by creating consistencies. So people may fall prey to any conspiracy theory that seems to explain reasonably (or unreasonably) what happened.

Confirmation bias: Once one has adopted some strange belief, confirmation bias serves to strengthen it. We tend to search for evidence that confirms our belief and ignore disconfirming evidence. We see this all the time in politics (for example, listening only to conservative/liberal media outlets), but it also helps strengthen outrageous theories and beliefs.

article continues after advertisement

With social media, it is very easy to find confirming information for any crazy theory or idea and simply ignore the mounds of disconfirming evidence. The result of confirmation bias, however, is that it can strengthen any outlandish belief.

Conformity processes: Believers of far-out conspiracy theories are in the minority, and the vast majority don’t hold those same weird beliefs. So, how can the conspiracy believer maintain their odd beliefs when most other people disbelieve? Well, research on conformity processes suggests that if you find other believers—even one person—it can help to strengthen the outrageous theory/belief. In fact, believers will often mention that there are others (“Many people believe…”).

Existential fears: Many conspiracy theories and outlandish beliefs involve threats to lives, personal safety, and democratic institutions. Many weird beliefs are an outgrowth of people’s fears about their own safety and mortality.

Audacious lies and belief systems: This comes from my research on lying. Often, the bigger and more audacious the lie, the more likely it is to be believed simply because the recipient figures, “If it’s that wild/unbelievable, it must be true!” This helps to draw in the believer and can be used to “convert” others to the weird belief system.

How to Counteract Someone’s Conspiracy Theory Beliefs?

As you can guess from the research, this is not easy given the believers’ extreme overconfidence and their tendency to believe that people agree with them. The antidote is to provide as much objective, contradictory evidence as you can. Although it may be discounted by the recipient, getting them to engage in some sort of critical thinking is the first step.

item.title: Want Calmer Arguments?
item.description:
Anger

Want Calmer Arguments?

Simple hacks to help you stay grounded as tensions rise.

Posted August 25, 2026

Key points
  • People want to be heard and understood, which is often where an argument starts: misunderstanding.
  • Rather than a full-blown argument, these small shifts can lead to more productive communication.
  • In many disagreements, both sides can feel or be “right” based on their perspective.
Source: RDNE Stock Project / Pexels

I remember a neighbor telling me what I thought and felt. His assumptions were inaccurate and insulting. When I tried to correct his perception, he did it again. It wasn’t a very long exchange, but it didn’t end well: I yelled and marched away.

Can you recall a confrontation where you lost your cool?

Arguments rarely appear "out of nowhere." Even if it feels like a sudden 0 to 100, there’s often a ramp-up and clues where things are headed. Pace, tone, emotions, a “need” to feel heard, or a desire to be right starts to build. Then, when the intensity passes a certain point, it can be hard to think clearly. Also, listening usually goes out the window, as does responding in ways that reflect who you want to be.

But if you actually want to think clearly, listen well, and respond in ways that reflect who you want to be, here are some tips that might support you. There's a tricky part, though: What may help you have better, calmer, more productive arguments can seem like the opposite of what feels natural in the moment.

Because I try (though imperfectly) to practice what I teach as a therapist, here are some of my favorite ways to intervene before a disagreement becomes a heated argument.

Start by Noticing 3 B’s: Body, Brain, and Breath

  1. Body: Notice if you're tensing up (tight jaw, clenched fists) or your speaking pace is picking up. These can be early clues of building tension that can result in a verbal explosion.
  2. Brain: You might catch your brain pushing to “win” or make your point. If either is happening, the interaction may be shifting from connection to escalation.
  3. Breath: Think about what happens as tension builds: Your breath changes. So if you catch that clue, before saying anything more, pause and take a long exhale. That small action may interrupt the argument’s momentum and give you a moment to choose what comes next.

From There, Take Action: Move to 4 S’s

  1. Slow your speech. Just when you may want to go faster and stronger, slowing down can make it harder to escalate. It can buy you time to better understand their position—time to formulate words that stop the escalation, time to own your feelings and rising temperature.
  2. Shoulders down. If they are pushed up toward your ears and that's not usual, you're probably quite tense—and your delivery will likely be, too. Intentionally lowering your shoulders may help reduce some of the urgency you feel inside.
  3. Soften your tone. As we build up, we tend to speak more firmly, loudly, or both, right? Even subtle changes in tone can shift the emotional temperature of a conversation.
  4. Speak with precision. Now is the time to shift your attention to your words. Choose them thoughtfully.

Language That Can Lower the Heat

When tensions rise, the immediate goal may not be to prove your point but to create conditions where a conversation or connection can continue. Phrases that might help foster more connection include:

  • “I want to hear you.”
  • “Please help me understand.”
  • “I care about you.”
  • “Can you help me understand what’s going on for you?”
  • "I'm noticing I'm not listening like I want to. Can we slow this down? I want to hear you."
  • "I think I'm hearing this: [State what you're taking in]. Is that correct?"

These statements—whichever best match the relationship and situation—signal openness and don’t require you to agree with their point. They communicate that the other person matters to you. The last one allows you to confirm your understanding of the exchange or situation before proceeding, which can give you time to choose where you go next. These kinds of statements may reduce the need for either party to push harder to be heard.

What Comes Next Matters

Using phrases like those above is not the end of the process; it can be the start of a different kind of engagement.

Set your point aside—just for a moment. This doesn’t mean abandoning your view, yourself, or your boundary. It also doesn't mean that you're shutting down, backing off, giving in, giving up, or "losing" the argument. Instead, it can help you manage the conversation so that understanding comes before responding. From there, you can re-engage more thoughtfully.

Looking back, had I used the last one—"I think I'm hearing you say X"—with my neighbor, it might have given me time to respond differently that day. How do I know? Because that's worked so many times before.

Sometimes asking helps to see the other’s point or simply to make sure the words and intention have been interpreted as meant. It can be the difference between reacting, often impulsively and defensively, and responding thoughtfully. Besides, in many disagreements, both sides can feel or be “right” based on their perspective.

To Use the Skills or Not to Use the Skills

Long before I yelled and marched away from my neighbor, my body gave me clues that things were going poorly. I remember feeling tired, stressed, and stretched that day. That's probably why I chose not to use the skills that have helped turn many potential arguments into productive conversations. (I mean those three B's and four S's—it's hard work!) So I went with the natural flow—and afterward, though I felt somewhat relieved after such an energy outburst, I also felt embarrassed a bit and hoped no one caught it on their cellphone video.

The person I was walking with has known me for decades. Once he caught up to my marching self, he said calmly, "I met a new part of you today."

Please note that these strategies would not likely apply to situations involving intimidation, abuse, or immediate danger; in those situations, disengaging and seeking safety may be more appropriate.
